courses.title: 1. CUDA C++ and the GPU model
courses.summary: Understand host vs device, write and launch your first kernel, and compile with nvcc.
courses.expected: Compiled with `nvcc cuda-intro.cu -o cuda-intro`, this launches four GPU threads, each printing its index; the order is not guaranteed.

lessons.title: Why GPUs, and the host/device split
paragraphs: A GPU runs thousands of lightweight threads in parallel, trading single-thread speed for massive throughput on data-parallel work. In CUDA C++ the CPU is the host and the GPU is the device; the host launches kernels that run on the device.
Host and device have separate memories, so data is explicitly transferred between them. This separation is the mental model behind every CUDA program.
lessons.example: // host code runs on the CPU; __global__ functions run on the GPU
lessons.pitfall: The GPU cannot read host (CPU) memory directly; you must allocate device memory and copy data over.

question.explanation: The host is the CPU; the device is the GPU.

lessons.title: Kernels and __global__
paragraphs: A kernel is a function marked `__global__` that runs on the device and is called from the host with the launch syntax `kernel<<<blocks, threads>>>(args)`. Every thread executes the same kernel body.
Kernel launches are asynchronous: the host continues immediately, so you synchronize with `cudaDeviceSynchronize()` before using results.
lessons.example:
__global__ void k(){ /* one thread's work */ }
k<<<1, 256>>>();
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting cudaDeviceSynchronize (or an error check) hides kernel errors and races with later host code.

question.prompt: Which qualifier marks a GPU kernel callable from the host?
question.explanation: __global__ functions are kernels launched from the host.

lessons.title: Compiling with nvcc
paragraphs: `nvcc` splits a .cu file into host code (handed to the host compiler) and device code (compiled to PTX/SASS for the GPU). You build with `nvcc file.cu -o file` and can target an architecture with `-arch=sm_80`.
nvcc links the CUDA runtime so the launch syntax and `cuda*` API calls resolve.
lessons.pitfall: Plain g++ cannot compile .cu kernels; use nvcc (or clang with CUDA support).

question.explanation: nvcc compiles .cu files, host and device.

lessons.title: Checking for errors
paragraphs: CUDA API calls return a `cudaError_t`; kernels report launch and runtime errors through `cudaGetLastError()` and `cudaDeviceSynchronize()`. Production code wraps calls in a macro that checks and reports.
Silent failures are the most common beginner trap, so check every call while learning.
lessons.example:
cudaError_t e = cudaGetLastError();
if (e) printf("%s\n", cudaGetErrorString(e));
lessons.pitfall: A kernel that 'does nothing' is often a launch that failed; always check cudaGetLastError after launch.

question.prompt: Kernel launch errors are retrieved with:
question.explanation: CUDA reports errors via cudaGetLastError and the returned codes.

courses.title: 2. Threads, blocks and grids
courses.summary: Index data with threadIdx, blockIdx and blockDim, and size a grid to cover an array.
courses.expected: Each thread computes a unique global index i and writes a[i]=i; the guard i<n protects the tail.

lessons.title: The thread hierarchy
paragraphs: CUDA threads are grouped into blocks, and blocks form a grid. Within a kernel, `threadIdx` gives the thread's position in its block, `blockIdx` the block's position in the grid, and `blockDim` the block size.
Blocks run independently and may execute in any order, which is why they must not depend on each other.
lessons.pitfall: Blocks cannot assume an execution order or communicate globally mid-kernel; design them independent.

question.explanation: blockDim is the block's thread count.

lessons.title: Computing a global index
paragraphs: The canonical 1-D global index is `blockIdx.x*blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`. It maps each thread to one element so the kernel is just the serial body with the loop replaced by the index.
Always compare the index against n before touching memory.
lessons.pitfall: An out-of-bounds thread writing past the array corrupts memory; the i<n guard is mandatory.

question.explanation: The last block may have extra threads beyond n.

lessons.title: Sizing the grid
paragraphs: To cover n elements with T threads per block you need ceil(n/T) blocks, written `(n + T - 1) / T`. Picking T as a multiple of 32 (the warp size), often 128 or 256, keeps the hardware busy.
The guard then handles the few extra threads in the final block.
lessons.pitfall: Using n/T (integer division) under-launches and skips the tail elements; use the ceiling form.

question.prompt: Blocks needed to cover n with T threads each:

lessons.title: Warps and divergence
paragraphs: Threads execute in warps of 32 in lockstep. When threads in a warp take different branch paths the warp serializes the paths, called divergence, which costs performance.
Keeping branches aligned to warp boundaries, or branchless, avoids most divergence.
lessons.pitfall: Heavy per-thread branching inside a warp silently halves throughput; measure before and after.

steps: Trace the global index for block 1, thread 5 with blockDim 256.
Explain why the i<n guard is required for the last block.

courses.title: 3. Memory: allocate, copy, and coalesce
courses.summary: Allocate device memory, move data with cudaMemcpy, and understand the memory spaces.
courses.expected: Host data is copied to the device, processed by a kernel, copied back, and the device buffer is freed.

lessons.title: Memory spaces
paragraphs: A GPU has global memory (large, high-latency, visible to all threads), shared memory (small, fast, per-block), registers (fastest, per-thread) and constant memory. Choosing the right space is the core of CUDA performance.
Most data lives in global memory; shared memory is an explicitly managed cache.
lessons.pitfall: Treating global memory like registers (many repeated loads) wastes bandwidth; stage reuse in shared memory.

question.explanation: Shared memory is fast and block-scoped.

lessons.title: cudaMalloc and cudaMemcpy
paragraphs: `cudaMalloc(&ptr, bytes)` allocates device memory; `cudaMemcpy(dst, src, bytes, kind)` transfers data with a direction such as `cudaMemcpyHostToDevice`. Device pointers must not be dereferenced on the host.
Free device memory with `cudaFree` to avoid leaks across many iterations.
lessons.pitfall: Passing the wrong copy direction, or a host pointer where a device pointer is expected, corrupts data silently.

lessons.title: Coalesced access
paragraphs: Global memory is fastest when consecutive threads read consecutive addresses, so a warp's 32 accesses merge into few transactions. This is coalescing, and it often dominates kernel speed.
Row-major arrays indexed by the global thread index coalesce naturally.
lessons.example: y[i] = a[i]; // thread i touches element i -> coalesced
lessons.pitfall: Strided or transposed access (thread i touches a[i*stride]) breaks coalescing and can be many times slower.

question.prompt: Coalesced access means a warp's threads touch:
question.explanation: Consecutive addresses merge into few transactions.

lessons.title: Unified memory
paragraphs: `cudaMallocManaged` allocates memory accessible from host and device, migrated on demand by the driver. It simplifies code and is great for learning, though explicit copies can be faster for tuned kernels.
Unified memory still benefits from prefetch hints on large working sets.
lessons.example: float* a; cudaMallocManaged(&a, bytes); // use on host and device
lessons.pitfall: Unified memory is convenient but not automatically optimal; measure against explicit copies for hot paths.

question.explanation: Managed memory migrates between host and device.

steps: Allocate, copy, and free a device buffer on paper.
Explain which copy direction each cudaMemcpy uses.
Describe a coalesced vs a strided access pattern.
Rewrite the example using cudaMallocManaged.

courses.title: 4. Vector addition and grid-stride loops
courses.summary: Write the canonical data-parallel kernel and scale it with a grid-stride loop.
courses.expected: Each thread adds one or more elements via the grid-stride loop, covering any n with any launch size.

lessons.title: The vector-add kernel
paragraphs: Vector addition is the 'hello world' of data parallelism: element i of c is a[i]+b[i], and each thread does one element. It shows the index-then-guard pattern with real work.
The host allocates, copies inputs, launches, and copies the result back.
lessons.pitfall: Launching fewer threads than n without a loop leaves the tail unprocessed.

question.explanation: One element per thread, or a strided set with a loop.

lessons.title: Grid-stride loops
paragraphs: A grid-stride loop lets a fixed-size grid process arrays larger than the launch: each thread steps by `blockDim.x*gridDim.x` until it runs off the end. This decouples the launch configuration from n.
It also improves reuse and makes kernels robust to any input size.
lessons.example: for (int i=start; i<n; i += blockDim.x*gridDim.x) c[i]=a[i]+b[i];
lessons.pitfall: Hard-coding one element per thread ties the grid to n and breaks for larger inputs.

question.explanation: The total thread count is the stride.

lessons.title: Choosing a launch configuration
paragraphs: A common choice is 256 threads per block and enough blocks to saturate the GPU, often a multiple of the SM count. With a grid-stride loop, correctness no longer depends on the exact numbers.
Occupancy tools and `cudaOccupancyMaxPotentialBlockSize` can suggest good sizes.
lessons.pitfall: Oversizing the grid wastes nothing with a stride loop, but undersizing without a loop drops work.

question.prompt: With a grid-stride loop, correctness depends on:

options.text: the loop and bounds, not the exact launch

question.explanation: The loop covers any size regardless of launch.

lessons.title: Verifying results
paragraphs: Always validate a kernel against a CPU reference on small inputs before trusting it at scale. Compare with a tolerance for floating point and check a few boundary indices.
Correctness first, then measure and optimize.
lessons.pitfall: A fast kernel that is wrong is worthless; verify against a reference before optimizing.

courses.title: 5. Shared memory and tiled matrix multiply
courses.summary: Use __shared__ memory and __syncthreads to tile a matrix multiply and cut global traffic.
courses.expected: Each 16×16 block cooperatively loads tiles into shared memory and accumulates, reusing each loaded value 16 times.

lessons.title: Shared memory as a cache
paragraphs: Shared memory is a small, fast, per-block scratchpad you manage by hand. By staging reused data there, a block avoids repeated slow global loads, which is the key to compute-bound kernels.
Declare it with `__shared__` inside the kernel.
lessons.pitfall: Shared memory is tiny (tens of KB per block); oversizing it reduces occupancy or fails to launch.

lessons.title: __syncthreads barriers
paragraphs: `__syncthreads()` is a barrier: every thread in the block waits until all arrive, guaranteeing shared-memory writes are visible before reads. Tiled algorithms sync after loading a tile and after consuming it.
All threads must reach the same `__syncthreads`, so it cannot sit inside a divergent branch.
lessons.example: As[ty][tx]=...; __syncthreads(); // now safe to read As
lessons.pitfall: Calling __syncthreads in a branch only some threads take deadlocks the block.

options.text: all block threads reached the barrier

lessons.title: Tiling for reuse
paragraphs: Tiling splits the matrices into sub-blocks that fit in shared memory; each tile is loaded once and reused by every thread in the block. This turns an O(N) memory-per-output kernel into far fewer global loads.
The arithmetic intensity rises, moving the kernel from memory-bound toward compute-bound.
lessons.pitfall: Tiling without the barriers reads stale or partially-written tiles and produces wrong results.

lessons.title: Bank conflicts
paragraphs: Shared memory is divided into banks; if threads in a warp access the same bank (but different words) the accesses serialize, a bank conflict. Padding arrays or changing access patterns avoids it.
For many tiled kernels the default layout is already conflict-free.
lessons.pitfall: A transposed shared-memory access can hit one bank repeatedly; pad the inner dimension to spread it.

courses.title: 6. Parallel reductions and atomics
courses.summary: Sum an array in parallel with a tree reduction, warp shuffles and atomics.
courses.expected: Each block reduces its slice in shared memory with a halving tree, then atomically adds its partial sum to the global result.

lessons.title: Tree reduction
paragraphs: A reduction combines many values into one (sum, max, …). In parallel it is a binary tree: at each step half the threads add a partner, halving the active set until one value remains.
It runs in log2(n) steps instead of n.
lessons.pitfall: Reducing in global memory without shared staging is far slower and often races.

question.prompt: A parallel reduction takes how many steps?

lessons.title: Atomics
paragraphs: When many threads update one location, an atomic like `atomicAdd` serializes those updates so none are lost. Blocks use one atomic for their partial sum rather than atomics per element.
Atomics are correct but contended; minimize how often you use them.
lessons.pitfall: Using atomicAdd per element instead of per block creates massive contention and is slow.

lessons.title: Warp shuffles
paragraphs: Within a warp, `__shfl_down_sync` exchanges registers directly without shared memory, giving a fast final reduction step. Modern reductions do the last 32 elements with shuffles.
This avoids shared-memory traffic and extra barriers for the warp-level part.
lessons.pitfall: Using the wrong active mask in a *_sync shuffle gives undefined results on divergent warps.

lessons.title: Two-pass vs atomic finalize
paragraphs: Reductions either write one partial per block and launch a second kernel to combine them, or finalize with a single atomic per block. The two-pass version avoids atomics; the atomic version avoids a second launch.
Both are common; choose based on contention and problem size.
lessons.example: // pass 1: per-block partials; pass 2: reduce the partials
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting to initialize the output to zero before an atomic-finalize kernel corrupts the sum.

question.explanation: It combines partials in a second kernel instead.

courses.title: 7. Streams, events and overlap
courses.summary: Overlap copies and compute with streams, time kernels with events, and prefetch unified memory.
courses.expected: Work issued to a stream runs in order but can overlap with other streams; async copies need pinned host memory to overlap.

lessons.title: Streams
paragraphs: A stream is an ordered queue of GPU work; operations in one stream run in issue order, but different streams can run concurrently. Using multiple streams overlaps data transfer with computation.
The default stream (0) synchronizes with others unless you opt out.
lessons.pitfall: Async copies only overlap when the host memory is pinned (cudaHostAlloc); pageable memory serializes.

question.explanation: A stream is ordered; streams overlap each other.

lessons.title: Events and timing
paragraphs: CUDA events mark points in a stream; `cudaEventRecord` then `cudaEventElapsedTime` measures GPU time accurately, unlike CPU timers around async launches. Events also express cross-stream dependencies.
Time the kernel region, not the one-time setup, and warm up first.
lessons.pitfall: Timing an async kernel with a CPU clock measures launch overhead, not execution; use events.

lessons.title: Overlapping transfer and compute
paragraphs: Splitting data into chunks and pipelining copy-in, compute and copy-out across streams hides transfer latency behind computation. This can approach the GPU's compute roofline for transfer-heavy workloads.
Pinned memory and enough chunks make the overlap effective.
lessons.example: // chunk i: HtoD(i) | kernel(i) | DtoH(i) across streams
lessons.pitfall: Too few chunks or pageable memory leaves gaps; profile to confirm real overlap.

question.explanation: Concurrent streams over pinned buffers overlap.

lessons.title: Prefetching unified memory
paragraphs: With unified memory, `cudaMemPrefetchAsync` moves pages to the GPU before a kernel so it does not fault on first touch. Prefetch hints recover much of the performance of explicit copies.
`cudaMemAdvise` can further tune placement for read-mostly data.
lessons.pitfall: Relying on first-touch migration inside a hot kernel causes page-fault stalls; prefetch beforehand.

options.text: moving pages before the kernel needs them

courses.title: 8. CUDA libraries: Thrust and cuBLAS
courses.summary: Stop hand-writing kernels for standard work: use NVIDIA's tuned libraries — Thrust for STL-style parallel algorithms and cuBLAS for dense linear algebra.
courses.expected: Compiled with `nvcc libraries.cu -o libraries`, it adds two device vectors and reduces the result entirely through Thrust, printing 3145728 — no custom kernel written.

lessons.title: Don't reinvent the wheel
paragraphs: NVIDIA ships a deep library ecosystem that is tuned per GPU architecture and usually beats hand-written kernels: Thrust and CUB (parallel algorithms), cuBLAS (dense linear algebra), cuFFT (FFTs), cuSPARSE (sparse), cuRAND (random numbers) and cuDNN (deep learning).

The first question for any standard operation — a reduction, a sort, a matrix multiply, an FFT — is 'is there a library for this?'. Reaching for a custom kernel first wastes effort and usually underperforms.
lessons.example: reduction/sort -> Thrust/CUB; GEMM -> cuBLAS; FFT -> cuFFT; conv -> cuDNN.
lessons.pitfall: Hand-writing a matrix multiply or FFT and expecting to beat cuBLAS/cuFFT almost always loses; the libraries are heavily tuned.

question.prompt: For a standard dense matrix multiply you should first reach for:

lessons.title: Thrust: STL-style parallelism
paragraphs: Thrust is a header-only C++ template library (shipped with CUDA) modeled on the STL. `thrust::device_vector` manages device memory with RAII, and host-side calls like `transform`, `reduce`, `sort`, `inclusive_scan` and `count_if` launch tuned kernels for you.
You write familiar, high-level C++ and Thrust picks an efficient implementation. It is the fastest way to get correct, reasonably fast GPU code for common data-parallel patterns.
lessons.pitfall: Dereferencing a device_vector element on the host (v[i]) triggers a hidden device-to-host copy each time — fine for debugging, disastrous in a loop.

lessons.title: cuBLAS for linear algebra
paragraphs: cuBLAS implements the BLAS routines (SAXPY, SGEMM, ...) on the GPU. You create a handle, pass device pointers, and link with `-lcublas`. For big matrices it reaches a large fraction of the GPU's peak FLOPS — far beyond a naive custom kernel.
The classic gotcha: cuBLAS is column-major (Fortran order), while C/C++ arrays are row-major, so you often compute the transposed problem or set the transpose flags accordingly.
lessons.pitfall: Passing row-major C arrays to cuBLAS without accounting for its column-major convention silently computes the wrong (transposed) result.

question.prompt: A classic cuBLAS gotcha is that it expects matrices in:

lessons.title: Interop with your own kernels
paragraphs: Libraries and hand-written kernels mix freely because they all operate on device pointers. `thrust::raw_pointer_cast(v.data())` gives the raw pointer of a device_vector to pass into your own kernel or a cuBLAS call, and a bare `cudaMalloc` pointer can be wrapped for Thrust with `thrust::device_ptr`.
The practical rule: use a library for the standard pieces and hand-write only the custom step that no library covers, keeping the data on the device throughout.
lessons.pitfall: Copying data back to the host between a Thrust call and your own kernel throws away the whole point — keep it resident on the device.

courses.title: 9. Multi-GPU programming
courses.summary: Scale beyond one GPU: enumerate devices, split work across them, use peer-to-peer copies, and reach for NCCL collectives at cluster scale.
courses.expected: Prints the GPU count, then splits a million-element array across every GPU so each adds a different scalar; on a single-GPU machine the whole array gets +1 (h[0]=2).

lessons.title: Why go multi-GPU
paragraphs: A single GPU has a fixed memory capacity and throughput ceiling. Big models and datasets exceed one GPU, so you spread the work across several GPUs in a node (and across nodes). `cudaGetDeviceCount` reports how many are visible and `cudaSetDevice(d)` selects the active one.
Almost every CUDA runtime call — allocations, copies, launches — applies to the currently selected device, so multi-GPU code is organized as 'select a device, then issue its work'.
lessons.example: cudaGetDeviceCount(&n); for (d..) { cudaSetDevice(d); /* work on GPU d */ }
lessons.pitfall: Allocating on one device and launching a kernel on another (forgetting cudaSetDevice) gives an invalid-device-pointer error.

options.text: subsequent runtime calls on that host thread

lessons.title: Splitting the work
paragraphs: The simplest multi-GPU pattern is data parallelism: partition the data into one slice per GPU, give each device its own buffer and stream, and run the same kernel on each slice independently. Throughput scales with the number of GPUs when the work is embarrassingly parallel.
Each device needs its own allocations and its own stream; work on different devices runs concurrently. You synchronize each device before using its results.
lessons.example: per device d: cudaSetDevice(d); cudaMalloc; copy slice; launch; copy back.
lessons.pitfall: Reusing one device pointer across GPUs fails — each device has a separate address space; allocate per device.

lessons.title: Peer-to-peer access
paragraphs: GPUs in the same node can often read each other's memory directly. `cudaDeviceCanAccessPeer` checks it and `cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess` turns it on, letting `cudaMemcpyPeer` copy GPU-to-GPU over NVLink or PCIe without bouncing through host memory.
Peer access cuts latency and frees host bandwidth for exchanges between devices, which matters a lot for algorithms that must share partial results each step (halo exchange, all-reduce).
lessons.example: cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess(peer, 0); cudaMemcpyPeer(dst, dstDev, src, srcDev, bytes);
lessons.pitfall: Doing GPU-to-GPU transfers via a host staging buffer when peer access is available wastes PCIe bandwidth and latency.

lessons.title: Collectives with NCCL
paragraphs: At cluster scale, you don't hand-code GPU-to-GPU communication — you use NCCL, NVIDIA's collective communications library. It implements topology-aware all-reduce, broadcast, all-gather and reduce-scatter across many GPUs and nodes, over NVLink, PCIe and InfiniBand.

NCCL all-reduce is exactly what data-parallel training frameworks (such as PyTorch DistributedDataParallel) use to average gradients across GPUs. The art is overlapping that communication with computation so the network is not a bottleneck.
lessons.example: ncclAllReduce(sendbuf, recvbuf, count, ncclFloat, ncclSum, comm, stream);
lessons.pitfall: Running a communication collective without overlapping it with compute leaves GPUs idle waiting on the network, destroying scaling efficiency.

courses.title: 10. Capstone: a tuned, verified kernel
courses.summary: Combine indexing, memory, shared tiling, timing and verification into one small project.
courses.expected: The capstone assembles a correct, timed, verified SAXPY and a short performance write-up.

lessons.title: Plan and correctness
paragraphs: Start from a correct CPU reference, port it to a straightforward kernel, and verify with a tolerance on small sizes. Only then scale up and optimize.
A clear acceptance test makes optimization safe.
lessons.pitfall: Optimizing before you have a passing reference test hides regressions.

question.prompt: The first step of a CUDA project is:
question.explanation: Correctness and a test come first.

lessons.title: Measure, then optimize
paragraphs: Measure a baseline with events, identify whether the kernel is memory- or compute-bound, then apply the matching optimization (coalescing, tiling, occupancy). Re-measure after each change.
Report GB/s or GFLOP/s against the device's peak to know when to stop.
lessons.pitfall: Guessing the bottleneck wastes effort; measure before changing anything.

question.prompt: You decide which optimization to apply by:
question.explanation: Measure first, then target the bottleneck.

lessons.title: Occupancy and limits
paragraphs: Occupancy is the ratio of active warps to the hardware maximum, limited by registers and shared memory per block. Higher occupancy hides latency but is not always the top priority.
The occupancy API and profiler reports guide block-size choices.
lessons.pitfall: Chasing 100% occupancy can hurt if it forces register spills; balance it with per-thread work.

options.text: registers and shared memory per block

lessons.title: Writing it up
paragraphs: A good capstone reports the hardware, the method, the measured throughput versus peak, and the correctness test used. Reproducibility matters as much as the number.
State clearly what was and was not optimized.
lessons.example: // Report: device, ms, GB/s, % of peak, test passed
lessons.pitfall: A speedup with no correctness test or hardware context is not a credible result.
